questions.question: What is target typing of lambdas?
options: The compiler infers the type of the lambda parameter
The programmer must always specify the type explicitly
It is a mandatory compilation error
It is a technique for creating anonymous classes
explanations: Correct. Target typing allows the compiler to infer the type of the lambda parameters based on the context.
It is not always required to specify it; the compiler can infer it.
It is not an error.
It is not related to anonymous classes.

questions.question: What is a Method Reference?
options: Class::method — shorthand for a lambda that calls an existing method
A reference to a static variable
A type of inheritance
A way to declare an abstract method
explanations: Correct. A method reference (Class::method) is a shorthand way to write a lambda that simply invokes an existing method.
It is not only for static variables.
It has nothing to do with inheritance.
It is not for declaring abstract methods.

questions.question: What types of method references exist?
options: Static, bound, unbound, and constructor
Only static and dynamic
Only instance and class
Only constructor and destructor
explanations: Correct. There are four types: static (Class::staticMethod), bound (object::method), unbound (Class::method), and constructor (Class::new).
The concepts of static/dynamic do not exist as types of method references.
There are more types than just instance and class.
The concept of a destructor does not exist in Java.

questions.question: Can lambdas be nested in Java?
options: Yes, but it reduces code readability
No, Java does not allow it
Only if var is used
Only with recursive functions
explanations: Correct. Java allows nesting lambdas, but doing so reduces readability and it is recommended to avoid it.
Java does allow it.
It does not depend on var.
It is not limited to recursive functions.

questions.question: What is an effectively final variable?
options: A local variable that is not modified and can be used inside a lambda
A variable declared with the final keyword
A static variable
An instance variable
explanations: Correct. An effectively final variable is a local variable that is not modified after its initialization, and it can be captured in lambdas without needing to be declared as final.
It does not need the final keyword, although it shares the restriction of not being modified.
It is not because it is static.
Instance variables do not need to be effectively final to be used in lambdas.
